extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological criteria for formulating, justifying, and applying principles of analytical mechanics (statics and dynamics), including Lagrange's and D'Alembert's methods, treatment of constraints, and philosophical standards for scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanistic explanations over theological/teleological accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept teleological accounts (e.g., 'light travels by shortest time because of the Creator's wisdom') as scientific explanations; seek physical causes and mechanisms instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Light actually travels by all paths, but waves intensify on paths of stationary time — this mechanistic account explains the observation better than invoking a Creator. The text warns that adopting theological reasons foregoes further knowledge of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain phenomena in terms of removal of work rather than appealing to 'economy' of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When phenomena exhibit maximal or minimal properties, the important explanatory factor is the removal (or impossibility of further removal) of work, not an a priori economical tendency of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: the catenary minimizes the centre of gravity because further descent is impossible; liquids subject only to molecular forces minimize surface area because equilibrium prevents further diminution. The text argues that saying 'so much only occurs as forces and circumstances allow' is more correct and comprehensive than attributing economy to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require more stringent tests for more general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The more general a new principle and the wider its claimed scope, the more perfect and demanding the tests that should be required of it, in view of the possibility of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a philosophical standard for accepting broad principles in mechanics and science generally: broad scope increases the need for rigorous empirical and logical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate consideration of individual facts and the whole (system-level) view
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific progress requires alternating between study of individual (differential/elementary) facts and consideration of nature as a whole (integral properties); neither purely local nor purely global views suffice alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Galileo's laws, Huygens's methods, and the concept of mass were obtained by such alternation. The text emphasizes that elementary laws never exist in absolute isolation because properties of one mass include relations to others (time relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit inquiry to what is accessible to exact investigation, and revise when new provinces open
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical science investigates only those things that are accessible to exact investigation; however, if previously inaccessible provinces become open to exact methods, scientists should then pursue inquiry and revise opinions accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses scientific modesty: avoid speculation beyond exact research, but be ready to exchange opinions for positive knowledge when methods and data permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer incomplete testable conceptions to apparently perfect but inadequate views
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest scientific attitude is toleration of an incomplete conception of the world and preference for it over an apparently perfect but inadequate conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical criterion encourages working with provisional, testable frameworks rather than imposing grand but untestable models (e.g., mechanical mythology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish synthetic (geometrical) and analytic (algebraic) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetic methods deduce results from given suppositions by geometrical constructions; analytic methods seek the conditions of a proposition (use algebra), and are commonly called 'analytical mechanics' when applied to mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's mechanics is described as synthetic/geometrical; the algebraical (analytical) method became usual after application of algebra to geometry and affords different procedural advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for economy, symmetry, and perspicuity in analytical formulations (Lagrange's aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good analytical mechanics should embody as much of the necessary reasoning as possible in concise, highly symmetrical, and perspicuous formulae, reducing remaining reasoning to mechanical procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lagrange's Mecanique analytique sought to 'dispose once for all of the reasoning necessary' by a single formula so that particular cases can be handled mechanically. This is presented as a virtue: economy of thought and simplicity of method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the principle of virtual velocities for statics: total virtual work = 0 for equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: For a system of material points with constraints, if the points receive infinitely small compatible displacements, then for equilibrium the sum of the work of impressed forces corresponding to those virtual displacements is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally: sum over points of (X dx + Y dy + Z dz) = 0; when forces are partial derivatives of a single function V, the total variation δV = 0 implying extrema (max/min). The text shows how constraints reduce arbitrary displacements and lead to equations determining equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use D'Alembert's principle to derive dynamics by introducing effective (inertial) forces
rubrics_metrics.description: In dynamics, consider the impressed forces together with the negatives of the effective (inertial) forces so that, owing to the connections of the system, these are in equilibrium; applying the principle of virtual velocities then yields the fundamental equations of dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains construction: effective forces arise from accelerations; inserting the negative inertial forces into the virtual-work relation produces differential equations of motion (D'Alembert's form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat constraints by expressing variations F=0 and eliminate them systematically using indeterminate coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: When constraints relate coordinates (F=0), vary them to get relations among variations (δF=0) and employ indeterminate coefficients (multipliers) multiplied by the constraint-variations and added to the virtual-work equation; then set coefficients of arbitrary displacements to zero to obtain equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the standard Lagrange multipliers procedure (illustrated by the two-lever example): multiply each constraint's differential by an indeterminate coefficient (A, μ, ...) and add to the virtual-work expression to eliminate dependent variations mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time-dependent constraints by including work done by changing connections
rubrics_metrics.description: If constraints (connections) undergo changes in time, the changes of connections perform work; when applying virtual-work/D'Alembert relations to actual displacements one must add the forces that produce the changes of the connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a straight line guiding a mass moving while the line itself accelerates; the appropriate modification introduces additional terms and may change which displacements are arbitrary. The text shows how to modify equations when F contains time explicitly and how to proceed by varying only spatial coordinates and differentiating the constraint wrt time for substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that different mechanical principles are different aspects of the same facts and are interderivable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical principles (virtual work, vis viva, least action, etc.) express different aspects of the same underlying facts; one principle can be derived from another under appropriate conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from D'Alembert's principle (virtual displacements) and when constraints are time-independent (actual motions = virtual), one can derive the principle of vis viva. The text emphasizes consistency and mutual derivability among principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve forces into components along fixed coordinate directions for symmetry and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve curvilinear forces into components in three fixed directions (rather than tangential/normal) to gain symmetry and perspicuity in computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Maclaurin's advance: resolving forces into fixed-direction components invests computations with a high degree of symmetry and clarity; recommended as a methodological choice in analytical mechanics.
